claim: Humans can read and comprehend text rapidly.
source: Humans can read and comprehend text rapidly, implying that readers might process multiple words per fixation.
evidence: This is a general statement about human reading ability that is part of established scientific knowledge in reading research.

claim: Readers might process multiple words per fixation.
source: Humans can read and comprehend text rapidly, implying that readers might process multiple words per fixation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that humans read rapidly, suggesting parallel processing.

claim: Participants silently read one-line sentences while brain activity and eye movements were recorded using MEG and an eye tracker.
source: We investigated parafoveal processing during natural reading by recording brain activity and eye movements using MEG and an eye tracker while participants silently read one-line sentences.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The sentences contained an unpredictable target word that was either congruent or incongruent with the sentence context.
source: The sentences contained an unpredictable target word that was either congruent or incongruent with the sentence context.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus characteristics.

claim: Target words were flickered at 60 Hz to measure parafoveal processing.
source: To measure parafoveal processing, we flickered the target words at 60 Hz and measured the resulting brain responses (i.e. Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging, RIFT) during fixations on the pre-target words.
evidence: This describes the RIFT technique used in the study.

claim: There was a significantly weaker tagging response for target words that were incongruent with the previous context compared to congruent ones.
source: Our results revealed a significantly weaker tagging response for target words that were incongruent with the previous context compared to congruent ones, even within 100ms of fixating the word immediately preceding the target.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The reduction in RIFT response for incongruent words was observed within 100ms of fixating the word immediately preceding the target.
source: Our results revealed a significantly weaker tagging response for target words that were incongruent with the previous context compared to congruent ones, even within 100ms of fixating the word immediately preceding the target.
evidence: This is a temporal finding from the data analysis.

claim: The reduction in the RIFT response was predictive of individual reading speed.
source: This reduction in the RIFT response was also found to be predictive of individual reading speed.
evidence: This is a correlation finding from the data analysis.

claim: Semantic information is not only extracted from the parafovea but can also be integrated with the previous context before the word is fixated.
source: We conclude that semantic information is not only extracted from the parafovea but can also be integrated with the previous context before the word is fixated.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Early and extensive parafoveal processing supports the rapid word processing required for natural reading.
source: This early and extensive parafoveal processing supports the rapid word processing required for natural reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of reading processes.

claim: Theoretical frameworks of natural reading should incorporate the concept of deep parafoveal processing.
source: Our study suggests that theoretical frameworks of natural reading should incorporate the concept of deep parafoveal processing.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Readers typically fixate each word for only 225–250ms during reading.
source: We typically fixate each word for only 225–250ms, but nevertheless manage to encode its visual information, extract its meaning, and integrate it into the larger context, while also doing saccade planning (Rayner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Readers manage to encode visual information, extract meaning, and integrate it into the larger context during brief fixations.

claim: Readers preview the next word in the parafovea before moving their eyes to it.
source: To overcome the tight temporal constraints during reading, we preview the next word in the parafovea before moving our eyes to it (Jensen et al., 2021; Reichle and Reingold, 2013; Schotter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Controversy remains about the extent and type of semantic information extracted from parafoveal processing.
source: However, for semantics in particular, controversy remains about the extent and type of information extracted from parafoveal processing under various conditions.
evidence: This reflects the current state of debate in the field.

claim: It is unknown when and how previewed semantic information can be integrated into the evolving sentence context.
source: Moreover, it is unknown when and how the previewed semantic information can be used – i.e., integrated into the evolving sentence context – which is an integral component of the ongoing reading process.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It was claimed that parafoveal preview was limited to perceptual features of words and did not extend to semantics.
source: For some time, it was claimed that parafoveal preview was limited to perceptual features of words and did not extend to semantics (Inhoff, 1982; Inhoff and Rayner, 1980; Rayner et al., 2014; Rayner et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Eye tracking-based evidence for the extraction of parafoveal semantic information began to emerge from studies in languages other than English.
source: However, eye tracking-based evidence for the extraction of parafoveal semantic information began to emerge from studies that used languages other than English, including Chinese (Tsai et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2013) and German (Hohenstein et al., 2010; Hohenstein and Kliegl, 2014), and was eventually extended into English (Rayner and Schotter, 2014; Schotter et al., 2015; Schotter and Jia, 2016; Veldre and Andrews, 2018; Veldre and Andrews, 2017; Veldre and Andrews, 2016a; Veldre and Andrews, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Schotter and Jia (2016) showed preview benefits on early gaze measures for plausible compared to implausible words.
source: For example, (Schotter and Jia, 2016) showed preview benefits on early gaze measures for plausible compared to implausible words, even for plausible words that were unrelated to the target.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The boundary paradigm makes it challenging to precisely determine when and how parafoveal semantic processing takes place.
source: However, due to the limitations of the boundary paradigm, which only assesses effects after target words have been fixated, it is challenging to precisely determine when and how parafoveal semantic processing takes place.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of a specific methodology.

claim: It is generally hard to distinguish between the effects of cross-saccade integration and the effects of how differing words fit into the context itself using the boundary paradigm.
source: Furthermore, it is generally hard to distinguish between the effects of cross-saccade integration (e.g. the mismatch between the preview and the word fixated) and the effects of how differing words fit into the context itself (Veldre and Andrews, 2016a; Veldre and Andrews, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Context-based facilitation of semantic processing can be observed as reductions in the amplitude of the N400 component.
source: Context-based facilitation of semantic processing can be observed as reductions in the amplitude of the N400 component (Kutas and Hillyard, 1984; Kutas and Hillyard, 1980), a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) response observed between about 300 and 500ms after stimulus onset, which has been linked to semantic access (DeLong et al., 2014; Federmeier, 2022; Federmeier et al., 2007; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Lau et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The N400 is a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) response observed between about 300 and 500ms after stimulus onset.
source: Context-based facilitation of semantic processing can be observed as reductions in the amplitude of the N400 component (Kutas and Hillyard, 1984; Kutas and Hillyard, 1980), a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) response observed between about 300 and 500ms after stimulus onset, which has been linked to semantic access (DeLong et al., 2014; Federmeier, 2022; Federmeier et al., 2007; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Lau et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The N400 has been linked to semantic access.
source: Context-based facilitation of semantic processing can be observed as reductions in the amplitude of the N400 component (Kutas and Hillyard, 1984; Kutas and Hillyard, 1980), a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) response observed between about 300 and 500ms after stimulus onset, which has been linked to semantic access (DeLong et al., 2014; Federmeier, 2022; Federmeier et al., 2007; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Lau et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Basic effects of contextual congruency on the N400 are observed for parafoveally-presented words.
source: Basic effects of contextual congruency on the N400 – smaller responses to words that do versus do not fit a sentence context (e.g. to 'butter' compared to 'socks' after 'He spread the warm bread with …') – are also observed for parafoveally-presented words (Antúnez et al., 2022; Barber et al., 2013; Barber et al., 2010; López-Peréz et al., 2016; Meade et al., 2021) and, even when all words are congruent, N400 responses to words in parafoveal preview, like those to foveated words, are graded by increasing context-based predictability (Payne et al., 2019; Payne and Federmeier, 2017; Stites et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: N400 responses to words in parafoveal preview are graded by increasing context-based predictability.
source: Basic effects of contextual congruency on the N400 – smaller responses to words that do versus do not fit a sentence context (e.g. to 'butter' compared to 'socks' after 'He spread the warm bread with …') – are also observed for parafoveally-presented words (Antúnez et al., 2022; Barber et al., 2013; Barber et al., 2010; López-Peréz et al., 2016; Meade et al., 2021) and, even when all words are congruent, N400 responses to words in parafoveal preview, like those to foveated words, are graded by increasing context-based predictability (Payne et al., 2019; Payne and Federmeier, 2017; Stites et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Similar N400 effects are obtained during natural reading.
source: Although many of these effects have been measured in the context of unnatural reading paradigms (e.g. the 'RSVP flanker paradigm'), similar effects are obtain during natural reading.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of different paradigms.

claim: Antúnez et al. (2022) showed that N400 responses were sensitive to the contextual plausibility of previewed words.
source: Using the stimuli and procedures from Schotter and Jia, 2016, Antúnez et al., 2022 showed that N400 responses, measured relative to the fixation before the target words i.e., before the boundary change while the manipulated words were in parafoveal preview, were sensitive to the contextual plausibility of these previewed words.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Semantic information is available from words before they are fixated.
source: These studies suggest that semantic information is available from words before they are fixated, even if that information does not always have an impact on eye fixation patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple studies.

claim: Semantic information from parafoveal preview does not always have an impact on eye fixation patterns.
source: These studies suggest that semantic information is available from words before they are fixated, even if that information does not always have an impact on eye fixation patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple studies.

claim: Most studies measuring parafoveal preview have been limited to fixations on an immediately adjacent word.
source: However, most of these studies have been limited to measuring parafoveal preview from fixations to an immediately adjacent word, raising questions about exactly how far in advance semantic information might become available from parafoveal preview.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of prior research.

claim: Some ERP studies have found that semantic information extracted from parafoveal preview is carried forward, affecting semantic processing when that same word is later fixated.
source: Although some ERP studies have found that the semantic information extracted from parafoveal preview is carried forward, affecting semantic processing when that same word is later fixated (Barber et al., 2010; Payne et al., 2019; Stites et al., 2017), other studies have not observed any downstream impact (Barber et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Other ERP studies have not observed any downstream impact of parafoveal semantic information.
source: Although some ERP studies have found that the semantic information extracted from parafoveal preview is carried forward, affecting semantic processing when that same word is later fixated (Barber et al., 2010; Payne et al., 2019; Stites et al., 2017), other studies have not observed any downstream impact (Barber et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Post-N400 ERP components do not seem to be elicited during parafoveal preview.
source: Furthermore, post-N400 ERP components, linked to more attentionally-demanding processes associated with message-building and revision, do not seem to be elicited during parafoveal preview (Li et al., 2023; Milligan et al., 2023; Payne et al., 2019; Schotter et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Post-N400 ERP components are linked to more attentionally-demanding processes associated with message-building and revision.
source: Furthermore, post-N400 ERP components, linked to more attentionally-demanding processes associated with message-building and revision, do not seem to be elicited during parafoveal preview (Li et al., 2023; Milligan et al., 2023; Payne et al., 2019; Schotter et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frequency tagging involves flickering a visual stimulus at a specific frequency and then measuring the neuronal response associated with processing the stimulus.
source: Frequency tagging, also known as steady-state visually evoked potentials, involves flickering a visual stimulus at a specific frequency and then measuring the neuronal response associated with processing the stimulus (Norcia et al., 2015; Vialatte et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frequency tagging has been widely used to investigate visuospatial attention.
source: It has been widely used to investigate visuospatial attention (Gulbinaite et al., 2019; Kritzman et al., 2022; Müller et al., 2003; Müller et al., 1998; Norcia et al., 2015; Vialatte et al., 2010) and has recently been applied to language processing (Beyersmann et al., 2021; Montani et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frequency tagging has recently been applied to language processing.
source: It has been widely used to investigate visuospatial attention (Gulbinaite et al., 2019; Kritzman et al., 2022; Müller et al., 2003; Müller et al., 1998; Norcia et al., 2015; Vialatte et al., 2010) and has recently been applied to language processing (Beyersmann et al., 2021; Montani et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2023).

source: To address this limitation, we developed the rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT) technique, which involves flickering visual stimuli at a frequency above 60 Hz, making it invisible and non-disruptive to the ongoing task.
evidence: This describes the RIFT technique developed by the authors.

source: This ensures a clear separation in processing the tagged word from the ongoing processing of other words, addressing a challenge faced by eye tracking and ERP/FRP approaches.
